overview: This five-page “List of Papers” is an archival index to State Department correspondence and memoranda concerning Japan’s automobile industry from 1934 through 1938. It traces Japanese efforts to foster and control domestic automobile production, the enactment and enforcement of the Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law, and its allegedly discriminatory effects on Ford and General Motors, alongside legal debate over American manufacturing rights under the 1911 treaty with Japan. Later entries cover Nissan’s development, Japanese production of cars and trucks, proposed American-Japanese ventures, Manchurian truck purchases, and the effects of the China Incident. Despite the broader file title, the surviving OCR contains no substantive material about carrier pigeons or bus lines.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Automobiles—Japan, sheets 1–5
subfiles.about: A five-sheet index summarizes State Department records on the development and regulation of Japan’s automobile industry between 1934 and 1938.
subfiles.summary: The index begins with statistics and forecasts for Japanese automobile production and proposals involving General Motors, then follows the drafting of legislation placing automobile manufacture under a licensing system. A substantial group of entries documents diplomatic representations and legal opinions concerning whether discriminatory controls violated Articles I and VII of the 1911 treaty with Japan. Subsequent entries trace passage and enforcement of the Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law, its impact on Ford and General Motors, and Nissan’s expansion. The final sheet points to reports on Japanese mass production, possible joint ventures serving Japan, China, and Manchukuo, rumored truck purchases in Manchuria, and the automobile industry during the China Incident; one National Foreign Trade Council entry is incomplete in the OCR.

interest: The index provides a compact chronology of Japan’s transition from dependence on American-assembled vehicles toward a protected, state-controlled domestic automobile industry. It is especially useful for tracing how commercial policy became a treaty issue: embassy conversations, State Department legal opinions, and references to Articles I and VII show disagreement over whether American individuals and corporations possessed equal manufacturing rights in Japan. The sheets also reveal where related reports were cross-filed and identify otherwise dispersed material on Ford, General Motors, Nissan, Manchuria, and the China Incident, although the underlying correspondence is not reproduced here.
